whyItExists.problem: A single Redis node is a single point of failure. If it goes down, your application loses its cache, sessions, or queue. Even with persistence, there's downtime for restart. High-traffic apps also need more capacity than one node.
whyItExists.solution: Redis Sentinel monitors a primary/replica pair and auto-promotes on failure (HA without sharding). Redis Cluster provides both HA and horizontal sharding across many nodes for truly large datasets.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Sentinel: when you need failover but dataset fits on one node. Cluster: when dataset exceeds one node's memory or you need extreme throughput.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Single-node Redis is simpler and handles 100GB+ and 1M+ ops/sec. Only add clustering when you have an actual capacity or availability requirement that single-node can't meet.

explainModes.beginner: Imagine a Redis that never goes down: Sentinel is a watchdog that notices when the main Redis crashes and quickly promotes a backup to take over. Cluster is like having multiple Redis boxes and splitting your data between them.
explainModes.simple: Sentinel: 3+ Sentinel processes monitor your primary. If the primary fails, they vote and promote a replica. Apps use the Sentinel address, not the primary address directly. Cluster: data is split into 16384 hash slots across 3+ nodes. Each node owns a range of slots.
explainModes.standard: Sentinel: Sentinels monitor via PING and vote to declare the primary down (quorum). They then trigger a failover: a replica is promoted, other replicas repoint to the new primary. Clients discover the current primary via the Sentinel. Cluster: 16384 hash slots, CRC16(key)%16384 determines slot. Nodes hold slot ranges and gossip cluster state. MOVED errors redirect clients to the correct node.
explainModes.technical: Sentinel uses a Raft-like quorum: needs ⌊N/2⌋+1 Sentinels to agree on failover (N=total sentinels). Sentinel leader election prevents split-brain. Cluster gossip uses PING/PONG with partial cluster state. A node is flagged PFAIL (probable failure) after CLUSTER_NODE_TIMEOUT, FAIL after a majority agrees. Replica promotion uses a Raft-like election among replicas of the failed primary.
explainModes.deepDive: Cluster supports read scaling via readonly replicas (READONLY command on the client connection). Multi-key commands require all keys in the same slot — use hash tags {tag} to co-locate. CLUSTER RESET wipes cluster state; CLUSTER REBALANCE redistributes slots. Managed Redis (ElastiCache, Upstash, Redis Cloud) abstracts away Sentinel/Cluster setup and provides automatic failover transparently.

content.text: Before Sentinel or Cluster, understand replication. A replica synchronises all writes from the primary in real time. Replicas serve reads, reduce load, and provide a failover target. But failover is manual without Sentinel.

content.code:
# Start a replica that replicates from primary at 6379
redis-server --port 6380 --replicaof 127.0.0.1 6379

# Check replication status
redis-cli -p 6379 INFO replication
# role:master
# connected_slaves:1
# slave0:ip=127.0.0.1,port=6380,state=online,offset=...

redis-cli -p 6380 INFO replication
# role:slave
# master_host:127.0.0.1
# master_port:6379
# master_link_status:up

content.text: Sentinel monitors the primary and replicas. When the primary fails, Sentinels vote and promote a replica automatically — typically within 10–30 seconds.

content.code:
# sentinel.conf (run 3 Sentinels for quorum of 2)
sentinel monitor mymaster 127.0.0.1 6379 2
# 2 = quorum (how many Sentinels must agree primary is down)

sentinel down-after-milliseconds mymaster 5000
# Mark primary down after 5 seconds of no response

sentinel failover-timeout mymaster 60000
# Failover must complete within 60 seconds

sentinel parallel-syncs mymaster 1
# Only 1 replica syncs with new primary at a time (reduces load)

# Start Sentinels
redis-sentinel sentinel.conf &
redis-sentinel sentinel2.conf &
redis-sentinel sentinel3.conf &

# Check Sentinel status
redis-cli -p 26379 SENTINEL masters
redis-cli -p 26379 SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name mymaster

content.text: Redis Cluster shards data across multiple nodes using 16384 hash slots. Each primary owns a slot range. Replicas provide failover. Keys route automatically via CRC16.

content.code:
# Check cluster health
redis-cli -p 7000 CLUSTER INFO
# cluster_state:ok
# cluster_slots_assigned:16384
# cluster_known_nodes:6

# See which nodes own which slots
redis-cli -p 7000 CLUSTER NODES

# See where a key would go
redis-cli -p 7000 CLUSTER KEYSLOT user:1    # slot number
redis-cli -p 7000 CLUSTER KEYSLOT user:2    # different slot

# Hash tags: force co-location
redis-cli -p 7000 CLUSTER KEYSLOT "{user:1}.name"   # same slot
redis-cli -p 7000 CLUSTER KEYSLOT "{user:1}.email"  # same slot

a.name: Redis Sentinel
a.useWhen: Need failover, dataset fits in one node (up to ~100GB)

b.name: Redis Cluster
b.useWhen: Dataset exceeds single node, or need extreme horizontal throughput

content.text: For most applications, start with Redis Sentinel (simpler, full compatibility). Only move to Cluster when your dataset exceeds single-node capacity. Many teams use managed Redis (AWS ElastiCache, Upstash, Redis Cloud) to avoid managing Sentinel or Cluster manually.

questions.question: What is Redis Sentinel used for?
options: Automatic failover for a primary/replica setup
questions.explanation: Sentinel monitors a primary/replica setup and automatically promotes a replica if the primary fails. It does not provide sharding — use Cluster for that.

questions.question: How does Redis Cluster route a key to the correct node?
options: CRC16(key) % 16384 determines the hash slot; each node owns a range of slots
The client remembers which node holds which key
All keys are on node 0; others are replicas
questions.explanation: Redis Cluster uses CRC16(key) % 16384 to map every key to one of 16384 hash slots. Each primary node owns a contiguous range of slots. The cluster-aware client routes commands to the correct node.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of primary nodes for a Redis Cluster?
questions.explanation: Redis Cluster requires at least 3 primary nodes to function correctly. This ensures that the cluster can reach a quorum for failure detection and slot rebalancing.

faq.q: Should I use Sentinel or Cluster?
faq.a: Use Sentinel for HA without sharding (simpler, full command compatibility). Use Cluster only when you need horizontal scale — your dataset doesn't fit in one node.

faq.q: What happens during a Sentinel failover?
faq.a: Sentinels detect the primary is down, vote to agree, elect a Sentinel leader, choose a replica to promote, reconfigure other replicas to follow the new primary, and notify clients. Total time: typically 10-30 seconds.

faq.q: How do managed Redis services handle HA?
faq.a: AWS ElastiCache, Redis Cloud, and Upstash abstract Sentinel/Cluster internally. ElastiCache offers 'Cluster Mode Disabled' (Sentinel-like) and 'Cluster Mode Enabled' (sharded Cluster). Failover is transparent to your application.

6-node Redis Cluster (3 primary + 3 replica) for a gaming platform needing 200GB cache
